authored.title: US intervention in Venezuela: A bold move for energy security and global energy dynamics? Lessons for Africa
authored.summary: Weighs the US operation in Venezuela as an energy-security move and draws lessons for African producers: balance resource nationalism with investor confidence, maintain infrastructure, diversify energy, and choose partnerships that serve national goals.
authored.pull_quote: Ultimately, the Venezuelan episode illustrates that energy security is not merely a function of resource endowments but of governance, investment, infrastructure, and geopolitical calculus.

authored.title: What the U.S.–Israel–Iran war means for Nigeria’s wallet
authored.summary: Traces how the conflict between the US, Israel and Iran reaches Nigeria through oil prices, Hormuz shipping risk, aviation disruption and investor flight, arguing higher crude helps only if output holds, while consumers still face costlier fuel and inflation.
authored.pull_quote: So the benefit may accrue “upstream” while the pain shows up “downstream” as higher transport costs, higher food prices, and higher inflation.

authored.title: Power to prosper: How energy transition can reduce poverty in Nigeria
authored.summary: Argues that renewables, especially off-grid solar, can cut energy poverty in Nigeria by widening access, creating jobs and lowering household costs, provided policy, cheap finance and community ownership support them.
authored.pull_quote: Energy transition is not just about saving the planet; for Nigeria, it’s about saving people from poverty.

authored.title: Africa’s energy future must be built on reality, not rhetoric
authored.summary: Contends Africa needs a pragmatic, home-defined transition: renewables alongside transitional gas, stronger grids and affordability, with fairer climate finance from rich nations rather than one-size-fits-all prescriptions.
authored.pull_quote: Pragmatism, not idealism, should guide Africa’s energy strategy.

authored.title: Taming the menace of open defecation in Nigeria
authored.summary: Argues that open defecation is a public health and economic drag on Nigeria, rooted in housing, culture and weak institutions, and calls for community-led sanitation, behavioural change and durable financing.
authored.pull_quote: Every naira spent on sanitation returns multiple times in saved healthcare costs, increased school attendance, and boosted productivity.

authored.title: Sanitation without accountability: Why Nigeria’s open defecation crisis persists (Part 2)
authored.summary: Argues that Nigeria’s open defecation persists because of weak accountability. It calls for empowered community committees, culturally aware messaging, integrated health and sanitation data, and state partnerships with proven local sanitation champions.
authored.pull_quote: Toilets are not just about waste; they are about dignity, equality, and state legitimacy.

authored.title: Filling up in a net-zero world: The fossil fuel paradox that won’t go away
authored.summary: Argues that continued investment in fuel stations reflects a non-linear energy transition. It calls for a pragmatic hybrid path: dual-use fuel and EV infrastructure, converting fleets first, and support for emerging markets.
authored.pull_quote: What we need is not ideological purity but pragmatic evolution.

authored.title: From station to destination: Is Nigeria’s fuel retail sector ready for the next level?
authored.summary: Argues that after subsidy removal, and with the Dangote Refinery reshaping supply, Nigerian fuel retailers must move beyond selling volume. They should compete on non-fuel retail, convenience, digital payments and loyalty, with regulators supporting the change.
authored.pull_quote: The pump is no longer enough. The question is simple: are we ready to go from station to destination?

authored.title: Turning Nigerians from consumers into owners
authored.summary: Argues the Dangote Refinery IPO could turn Nigerians from fuel consumers into owners, deepen the capital market, and test whether African savings can finance African industrialisation and energy security.
authored.pull_quote: It asks whether the next chapter of Africa’s development can be defined by what Africans build, what Africans finance and what Africans own.

authored.title: Divided by barrels, united by football
authored.summary: Uses the 2026 FIFA World Cup to argue that sport remains a valuable if symbolic channel of diplomacy and economic signalling in a world fragmented by geopolitical and energy rivalries.
authored.pull_quote: The world may remain divided by barrels, but it is still occasionally united by football.

authored.title: Nigeria’s unexpected shield in a time of global energy turbulence
authored.summary: Argues that the Dangote Refinery spared Nigeria a fuel crisis during the Middle East conflict, but warns against relying on one private asset and urges refinery sales, modular refineries and strategic reserves.
authored.pull_quote: Nations that fail to refine what they produce will always import the consequences of global instability.

mentions.title: What the MPC’s rate cut really signals
mentions.summary: Explains the Central Bank of Nigeria’s 50-basis-point cut to 26.5 per cent alongside an unchanged 45 per cent cash reserve ratio, reading it as cautious easing without releasing liquidity.
mentions.pull_quote: Olugbenga Olaoye, an energy economist, says, “This rate cut is not dramatic. It is small and cautious.”

mentions.title: Oil price surge tests Nigeria’s post-subsidy model
mentions.summary: Reports that, without fuel subsidies, rising crude prices pass straight into Nigerian fuel, transport and food costs, while limited refining means the country gains little from higher oil prices.
mentions.pull_quote: “The country exports crude but still imports fuel, so rising prices increase both revenues and costs at the same time.”

mentions.title: How 132 ships became none in Hormuz
mentions.summary: Analyses the collapse in Strait of Hormuz vessel crossings in early 2026, arguing that lost commercial confidence rather than formal closure drives freight, oil prices and imported inflation.
mentions.pull_quote: In his view, once confidence weakens, prices, freight decisions and hedging behaviour begin to adjust long before any formal shortage is visible.

mentions.title: How Nigeria’s debt bill is squeezing the budget
mentions.summary: BusinessDay Pro analysis showing debt service consumed about 67 per cent of federal revenue in early-to-late 2025, arguing a shallow revenue base, not the debt stock alone, is squeezing Nigeria’s budget.
mentions.pull_quote: “Nigeria is not being squeezed only by how much it owes. It is being squeezed by the cost of servicing what it owes against a revenue base that remains dangerously shallow,” said Olugbenga Olaoye, a member of the United States Association for Energy Economics (USAEE).

mentions.title: Nigeria’s oil windfall comes at a cost of living crisis for households
mentions.summary: Argues that Brent above $100 amid Middle East tensions boosts Nigeria’s oil revenues while raising fuel, transport and living costs for households and businesses.
mentions.pull_quote: “Higher oil prices improve government earnings, but they also increase costs across the economy.

mentions.title: Nigeria’s economy seen growing at fastest rate in 5 years
mentions.summary: Projects roughly 4 per cent first-quarter 2026 GDP growth as reform shocks fade, while noting growth remains too slow to cut poverty and energy-linked inflation makes recovery uneven.
mentions.pull_quote: “What we now have is a more uneven recovery where services and consumption continue to support activity, but energy-linked inflation pressures are slowing the transmission mechanism,” he said.

mentions.title: Oil at $100 again, but Nigeria is poorer for it this time
mentions.summary: Compares today’s $100 oil with the 1970s shocks, arguing Nigeria now absorbs price volatility faster through inflation and fuel costs, and recommending local refining, reliable power and renewables as buffers.
mentions.pull_quote: As Olugbenga Olaoye, energy economist and member of the United States Association for Energy Economics (USAEE), notes, “Nigeria’s inflation response to external oil shocks is no longer gradual.

mentions.title: Olivetian And Olivia Energy Boss, Gbenga Olaoye Tips Alumni On Compelling Opportunities To Grip In Covid-19 Era
mentions.summary: Reports a webinar in which he advised Olivet Baptist High School, Oyo alumni to start needs-driven businesses during Covid-19, such as logistics, home-office fit-outs, food and healthcare.
mentions.pull_quote: Business success is about meeting needs.

mentions.title: Oil price surge tests Nigeria’s post-subsidy model
mentions.summary: News analysis on how rising crude prices, with no subsidy left, now pass straight into Nigerian fuel, transport and food costs, while limited refining keeps the country dependent on fuel imports.
mentions.pull_quote: “This is why Nigeria is not fully benefiting from higher oil prices,” said Olugbenga Olaoye, an energy economist and member of USAEE.

mentions.title: Clinton School Students Embark on International Public Service Projects
mentions.summary: School news item listing student summer placements; it records him placed with International Development Enterprises in Denver, working on feedback and learning loops for its KPI systems.

mentions.title: Arkansas-Focused Practicum Projects Announced for 2023-24
mentions.summary: School news item announcing ten first-year student practicum teams for 2023-24; he is listed on the Encore Bank team studying homeownership barriers for majority-minority communities. Not energy commentary.

mentions.title: Africa exports raw wealth, imports global shocks
mentions.summary: Reports that Sub-Saharan Africa’s reliance on unprocessed commodity exports leaves it exposed to global shocks, citing Nigeria’s Dangote Refinery as evidence that local value addition cushions economies.
mentions.pull_quote: Olugbenga Olaoye, energy economist and member of the USAEE, says, “For decades, Nigeria operated a structurally flawed downstream model: exporting crude oil while importing refined products.

mentions.title: UAE exit deepens OPEC’s fading pricing influence
mentions.summary: Analyses how the UAE’s departure from OPEC weakens the cartel’s supply discipline and argues that Nigeria, hampered by volatile output, remains a price-dependent producer with little volume flexibility.
mentions.pull_quote: According to Olugbenga Olaoye, Nigeria’s gains reflect short-term efficiency improvements rather than a durable expansion in capacity.

mentions.title: UAE exit from OPEC exposes Nigeria’s structural output limits
mentions.summary: Argues that the UAE leaving OPEC weakens the cartel’s pricing power and exposes Nigeria as a price-dependent producer unable to raise output, straining revenue projections and budgets.
mentions.pull_quote: According to Olugbenga Olaoye, Nigeria’s gains reflect short-term efficiency improvements rather than a durable expansion in capacity.

mentions.title: Rising oil prices tighten CBN’s options, deepen growth–inflation trade-off
mentions.summary: Argues that rising oil prices leave Nigeria’s central bank facing a costly trade-off between containing inflation and supporting growth, with holding, tightening and easing each carrying risks.
mentions.pull_quote: Olugbenga Olaoye, energy economist, observes that delayed responses to global shocks allow cost pressures to cascade across sectors.

mentions.title: Dangote–PENGASSAN tensions may spark new economic threat
mentions.summary: Argues that the standoff between the Dangote refinery and the PENGASSAN oil union could disrupt fuel supply, push up prices and inflation, and jeopardise gains from Nigeria’s recent reforms.
mentions.pull_quote: Over the years, unions such as PENGASSAN have appeared inevitable and untouchable, but at this level, unionism undermines national stability.
